record.question:
A company uses a provisioned Amazon Redshift cluster encrypted with AWS KMS. Its disaster recovery policy requires encrypted snapshot copies in a second AWS Region more than 500 miles away. The destination must use a customer managed KMS key, and the team will configure the workflow through the CLI. The recovery objective permits restoring a new cluster from the latest copied snapshot.

Which solution meets these requirements with the least ongoing operational effort?

options.text: Locate the Redshift-managed snapshot objects in an S3 bucket and enable S3 Cross-Region Replication to a bucket encrypted with the destination KMS key.

Create a snapshot copy grant in the destination Region for its customer managed KMS key. Enable Redshift cross-Region snapshot copy on the source cluster with that grant and configure snapshot retention.

Keep cross-Region snapshot copy disabled. Schedule a Lambda function to call CopyClusterSnapshot on each new automated snapshot, and retain the resulting manual snapshots as the disaster recovery copies.
Enable cross-Region snapshot copy and specify the destination customer managed KMS key, but omit the destination snapshot copy grant because the source cluster is already encrypted.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. Redshift's managed cross-Region snapshot-copy feature continuously handles eligible snapshot copies after configuration. For a destination customer managed KMS key, the snapshot copy grant authorizes use of that key. The copied snapshot is encrypted in the destination Region and can be used to restore a new cluster.

<<1>> assumes that Redshift-managed snapshots are customer-controlled S3 objects to which an ordinary bucket replication rule can be attached. Use the Redshift snapshot-copy feature instead.

<<3>> preserves automated snapshots as manual snapshots in the same Region. CopyClusterSnapshot does not perform the required cross-Region copy, so those copies do not meet the geographic separation requirement.

<<4>> omits the grant required by the specified destination key choice. Source encryption does not grant permission to use a separate destination customer managed key.

Snapshot copying is a backup-and-restore DR strategy, not an already running failover cluster. Set retention, monitor copy completion, and test restore times against the recovery objectives. A snapshot copy grant is not required when the destination uses a Region-owned key, which is why this scenario explicitly specifies a customer managed key.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Redshift encrypted snapshot copies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/redshift/latest/mgmt/working-with-db-encryption.html); [Redshift cross-Region snapshot copy](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/redshift/latest/mgmt/cross-region-snapshot-copy.html). [CopyClusterSnapshot API](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/redshift/latest/APIReference/API_CopyClusterSnapshot.html).

diagram_alt: The destination copy grant authorizes its KMS key, while the copied snapshot remains a backup that must be restored for recovery.

sources.supports: Cross-Region copies re-encrypt snapshots with destination key material, and a destination customer managed KMS key requires a snapshot copy grant.
Redshift can automatically copy snapshots to one destination Region with configured retention for later cluster restoration.
CopyClusterSnapshot converts an automated snapshot to a manual snapshot and has no destination Region parameter.

editorial_notes: Preserved answer 2. Corrected the blanket claim that every encrypted cross-Region copy needs a grant by explicitly requiring a destination customer managed key. Distinguished managed snapshot DR from immediate failover.
Root replaced a claimed custom cross-Region copy workflow with a concrete wrong-API distractor after reviewing CopyClusterSnapshot API parameters.
